These exercises reproduce lectures 16 and 17. The first two parts use the order book data of SPY, the exchange-traded fund on the S&P 500: liquidity through the day and over the years, price impact, and the bid-ask bounce, which leads to the microstructure noise of lecture 17. The last two parts use VOLARE, the daily realized measures of the E-mini S&P 500 futures (ES) and the 30 Dow Jones stocks: they measure volatility and forecast it with the HAR model. The third assignment works with the same data. All tasks come with complete solutions, so you can work through them on your own.

## Liquidity and price impact of SPY

**Exercises:**

1. Download the SPY order book snapshots for March of every year from 2008 to 2025 with `download_data(domain = "Tidy Finance", dataset = "high_frequency_sp500")` from `tidyfinance`. What does one row contain, and in which units are the spread, the depth and the volume?
2. Liquidity through the day: for March 2024, compute the median spread, the median depth at the best quotes in USD, and the median dollar volume per five seconds in each ten-minute interval of continuous trading, and plot them against the time of day. Leave out the snapshots of the opening and closing auctions. What pattern do you see, and why? Why do the lecture's figures show medians instead of means?
3. Liquidity over the years: compute the average spread and depth for each March. How did they change since 2008, and which years stand out?
4. Price impact (Kyle, 1985): aggregate the snapshots to one-minute midquote returns in basis points and one-minute net buying in USD million (`signed_volume`, which is in shares, times the midquote), and regress the returns on the net buying, year by year. How does the slope $\lambda$, the price impact of USD 1 million of net buying, change over time, and how does the $R^2$? What do your results mean for the trading costs of a portfolio of large stocks, as in lecture 5?

**Solutions:**

The snapshots are taken every five seconds during regular trading hours of NASDAQ, built from LOBSTER data. One month of SPY has about 100,000 rows, so the 18 months take a moment to download.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-download-spy
library(tidyverse)
library(tidyfinance)
library(scales)

years <- 2008:2025
sample_month <- 3

spy <- map(years, \(year) {
  start <- make_date(year, sample_month, 1)
  download_data(
    domain = "Tidy Finance",
    dataset = "high_frequency_sp500",
    start_date = start,
    end_date = ceiling_date(start, "month") - days(1)
  ) |>
    mutate(year = year)
}) |>
  bind_rows()

glimpse(spy)
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-download-spy
from calendar import monthrange
from datetime import date

import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import tidyfinance as tf
from plotnine import *

years = range(2008, 2026)
sample_month = 3

spy = pl.concat(
    tf.download_data(
        domain="Tidy Finance",
        dataset="high_frequency_sp500",
        start_date=date(year, sample_month, 1),
        end_date=date(year, sample_month, monthrange(year, sample_month)[1]),
    ).with_columns(year=pl.lit(year))
    for year in years
)

spy.glimpse()
```
:::

The 18 months have 1,815,840 snapshots. Each row is one snapshot `ts` of the order book: the `midquote` in USD, the `spread` in basis points of the midquote, the depth at the best ask and bid (`depth0_ask`, `depth0_bid`) and within 5 basis points of the midquote (`depth5_ask`, `depth5_bid`) in shares, the dollar volume traded in the five seconds before (`trading_volume`), and the signed order flow (`signed_volume`), buyer- minus seller-initiated shares. Shares times the midquote give USD.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-intraday
recent_year <- 2024
bucket_minutes <- 10

intraday <- spy |>
  filter(year == recent_year) |>
  mutate(clock_exact = hour(ts) + minute(ts) / 60 + second(ts) / 3600) |>
  filter(clock_exact > 9.5 + 5 / 3600, clock_exact < 16) |>
  mutate(
    time = floor_date(ts, paste(bucket_minutes, "minutes")),
    clock = hour(time) + minute(time) / 60
  ) |>
  summarize(
    spread = median(spread),
    depth = median((depth0_ask + depth0_bid) / 2 * midquote),
    volume = median(trading_volume),
    .by = clock
  )

intraday |>
  pivot_longer(-clock) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = clock, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Hour of the day (New York time)", y = NULL)
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-intraday
recent_year = 2024
bucket_minutes = 10

clock_exact = (
    pl.col("ts").dt.hour()
    + pl.col("ts").dt.minute() / 60
    + pl.col("ts").dt.second() / 3600
)
time = pl.col("ts").dt.truncate(f"{bucket_minutes}m")

intraday = (
    spy.filter(
        pl.col("year") == recent_year, clock_exact > 9.5 + 5 / 3600, clock_exact < 16
    )
    .group_by(clock=time.dt.hour() + time.dt.minute() / 60)
    .agg(
        spread=pl.col("spread").median(),
        depth=(
            (pl.col("depth0_ask") + pl.col("depth0_bid")) / 2 * pl.col("midquote")
        ).median(),
        volume=pl.col("trading_volume").median(),
    )
    .sort("clock")
)

(
    ggplot(intraday.unpivot(index="clock"), aes(x="clock", y="value"))
    + geom_line()
    + facet_wrap("variable", scales="free_y")
    + labs(x="Hour of the day (New York time)", y="")
)
```
:::

The snapshot at 9:30:05 still holds the opening auction and the one at 16:00:00 the closing auction, so the filter keeps the continuous trading from 9:30:10 to 15:59:55, as in lectures 16 and 17. In March 2024, trading is heaviest at the open and at the close: the median dollar volume per five seconds falls from about USD 1.5 million in the first ten minutes to about USD 0.4 million in the early afternoon and rises to USD 4.7 million in the last ten minutes (the U-shape). The spread is widest right after the open (0.23 basis points), when uncertainty about the day's news is largest, and stays close to 0.20 basis points from noon on. Depth at the best quotes builds up during the day, from about USD 0.22 million in the first ten minutes to 0.30 million in the afternoon and 0.43 million in the last ten minutes.

The figures show medians, as in lecture 16, because a mean follows the few days with news in an interval, such as the Fed's statement on 20 March 2024 (lecture 16). The means are higher: USD 2.0 million instead of 1.5 million in the first ten minutes, and USD 6.5 million instead of 4.7 million in the last ten.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-yearly
yearly <- spy |>
  summarize(
    spread = mean(spread),
    depth = mean((depth0_ask + depth0_bid) / 2 * midquote),
    .by = year
  )

yearly |>
  pivot_longer(-year) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-yearly
yearly = (
    spy.group_by("year")
    .agg(
        spread=pl.col("spread").mean(),
        depth=(
            (pl.col("depth0_ask") + pl.col("depth0_bid")) / 2 * pl.col("midquote")
        ).mean(),
    )
    .sort("year")
)

(
    ggplot(yearly.unpivot(index="year"), aes(x="year", y="value"))
    + geom_line()
    + geom_point()
    + facet_wrap("variable", scales="free_y")
    + labs(x="", y="")
)
```
:::

The spread fell from 0.91 basis points in March 2008 to 0.21 in March 2024, and rose again to 0.50 in March 2025. SPY trades at the minimum tick of one cent, and with a rising price, one cent became an ever smaller share of the price. The crisis months stand out: 1.49 basis points in March 2009, after the Lehman collapse, and 0.86 in March 2020, during the COVID-19 crash. Depth at the best quotes fell as well, from about USD 1.1 million in 2008 to 0.3 million in 2024, with a low of USD 0.05 million in March 2020: orders are smaller and spread over more trading venues.

For the price impact, the last midquote of each minute gives the minute's return. The signed volume is in shares; times the midquote of its snapshot and summed over the minute, it gives the minute's net buying in USD million. Returns are computed within a day, so the overnight change does not count as a one-minute return.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-price-impact
interval_length <- "1 minute"

price_impact <- spy |>
  mutate(day = as_date(ts), minute = floor_date(ts, interval_length)) |>
  summarize(
    flow = sum(signed_volume * midquote) / 1e6,
    midquote = last(midquote),
    .by = c(year, day, minute)
  ) |>
  mutate(ret = 1e4 * log(midquote / lag(midquote)), .by = c(year, day)) |>
  drop_na() |>
  nest(data = -year) |>
  mutate(
    fit = map(data, \(d) lm(ret ~ flow, data = d)),
    lambda = map_dbl(fit, \(f) coef(f)[["flow"]]),
    r2 = map_dbl(fit, \(f) summary(f)$r.squared)
  ) |>
  select(year, lambda, r2)

price_impact
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-price-impact
interval_length = "1m"

price_impact = (
    spy.with_columns(
        day=pl.col("ts").dt.date(), minute=pl.col("ts").dt.truncate(interval_length)
    )
    .group_by("year", "day", "minute", maintain_order=True)
    .agg(
        flow=(pl.col("signed_volume") * pl.col("midquote")).sum() / 1e6,
        midquote=pl.col("midquote").last(),
    )
    .sort("year", "day", "minute")
    .with_columns(ret=1e4 * pl.col("midquote").log().diff().over("year", "day"))
    .drop_nulls()
    .group_by("year", maintain_order=True)
    .agg(
        lambda_=pl.cov("ret", "flow") / pl.col("flow").var(),
        r2=pl.corr("ret", "flow") ** 2,
    )
)
price_impact
```
:::

With one regressor, the slope is the covariance of returns and order flow divided by the variance of the order flow, and the $R^2$ is their squared correlation, so the Python code computes them directly.

USD 1 million of net buying in a minute moved SPY by 0.34 basis points in March 2008, by 0.24 in March 2024 and by 0.58 in March 2025. In the other years it lay between 0.18 and 0.83 basis points, except in the crisis months: 1.19 basis points in March 2009 and 1.84 in March 2020. The $R^2$ fell from between 12% and 40% until 2012 to between 1% and 8% since 2020: more and more of the price moves without trading in SPY, as quotes react to news and to trading on other venues. For a portfolio of large stocks, net buying of USD 1 million costs a fraction of a basis point in calm months, so the quadratic costs of lecture 5 matter mostly for large trades and in crises.

## The bid-ask bounce

**Exercises:**

5. Roll (1984): the true price $m_t$ follows a random walk, and each trade happens at the bid or at the ask with equal probability, $p_t = m_t + \frac{s}{2} q_t$ with $q_t = \pm 1$. Simulate 10,000 trades with a spread $s$ of two cents, a true price that starts at USD 100 and moves by a normal change with a standard deviation of half a cent per trade. Plot the first 40 trade prices together with the true price, compute the autocovariance of the trade price changes, $\text{Cov}(\Delta p_t, \Delta p_{t-1})$, and recover the spread with Roll's formula $s = 2\sqrt{-\text{Cov}(\Delta p_t, \Delta p_{t-1})}$.
6. Compute the variance of the trade price changes and of the changes of the true price. How much of the variance of the trade price changes is bid-ask bounce, and what happens to this share if you sample every 10th or every 100th trade instead of every trade? Why does this matter for volatility measured from high-frequency data (lecture 17)?

**Solutions:**

The simulation draws the true price changes and the sides of the trades; the seed makes the draws reproducible. Changes are in cents, as in lecture 16.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-roll
n_trades <- 10000
true_spread <- 0.02
price_volatility <- 0.005
start_price <- 100
n_shown <- 40

set.seed(1984)
roll <- tibble(
  trade = 1:n_trades,
  true_price = start_price + cumsum(rnorm(n_trades, sd = price_volatility)),
  side = sample(c(-1, 1), n_trades, replace = TRUE),
  trade_price = true_price + true_spread / 2 * side
) |>
  mutate(
    change = 100 * (trade_price - lag(trade_price)),
    previous_change = lag(change)
  )

roll |>
  filter(trade <= n_shown) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = trade)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = true_price)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = trade_price), color = "#901A1E") +
  labs(x = "Trade", y = "Price (USD)")

autocovariance <- cov(roll$change, roll$previous_change, use = "complete.obs")
c(autocovariance = autocovariance, roll_spread = 2 * sqrt(-autocovariance))
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-roll
n_trades = 10_000
true_spread = 0.02
price_volatility = 0.005
start_price = 100
n_shown = 40

rng = np.random.default_rng(1984)
true_price = start_price + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, price_volatility, n_trades))
side = rng.choice([-1, 1], n_trades)
roll = (
    pl.DataFrame(
        {
            "trade": np.arange(1, n_trades + 1),
            "true_price": true_price,
            "trade_price": true_price + true_spread / 2 * side,
        }
    )
    .with_columns(change=100 * pl.col("trade_price").diff())
    .with_columns(previous_change=pl.col("change").shift(1))
)

(
    ggplot(roll.filter(pl.col("trade") <= n_shown), aes(x="trade"))
    + geom_line(aes(y="true_price"))
    + geom_point(aes(y="trade_price"), color="#901A1E")
    + labs(x="Trade", y="Price (USD)")
)
```

```{python}
#| label: py-roll-spread
autocovariance = roll.drop_nulls().select(pl.cov("change", "previous_change")).item()
{"autocovariance": autocovariance, "roll_spread": 2 * np.sqrt(-autocovariance)}
```
:::

In R, the autocovariance of the trade price changes is −0.97 cents² (theory: $-s^2/4 = -1$ cent²), so Roll's formula gives a spread of 1.97 cents, close to the true 2 cents; these are the numbers of lecture 16. Python draws other random numbers from the same seed, so its numbers differ a little: −1.03 cents² and 2.03 cents. In the figure, the trade price jumps between the bid and the ask around the true price: after a trade at the ask, the next trade price tends to fall, after a trade at the bid it tends to rise.

For the variances, we keep every $k$-th trade and compute the price changes between the trades we keep. The bounce adds the same variance $s^2/2$ to every price change, however long the interval between the trades, while the variance of the true price grows with the number of trades in between.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-roll-sampling
sampling_steps <- c(1, 10, 100)

map(sampling_steps, \(step) {
  sampled <- roll |> filter(trade %% step == 0)
  tibble(
    every_kth_trade = step,
    trade_price_variance = var(100 * diff(sampled$trade_price)),
    true_price_variance = var(100 * diff(sampled$true_price))
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(bounce_share = 1 - true_price_variance / trade_price_variance)
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-roll-sampling
sampling_steps = [1, 10, 100]

pl.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "every_kth_trade": step,
            "trade_price_variance": np.var(
                100 * np.diff(sampled["trade_price"]), ddof=1
            ),
            "true_price_variance": np.var(100 * np.diff(sampled["true_price"]), ddof=1),
        }
        for step in sampling_steps
        for sampled in [roll.filter(pl.col("trade") % step == 0)]
    ]
).with_columns(
    bounce_share=1 - pl.col("true_price_variance") / pl.col("trade_price_variance")
)
```
:::

| Trades | Variance of trade price changes (cents²) | Variance of true price changes (cents²) | Share of the bounce |
|:-------|----:|----:|----:|
| Every trade | 2.24 (Python: 2.27) | 0.25 (0.25) | 89% (89%) |
| Every 10th trade | 4.58 (4.31) | 2.37 (2.55) | 48% (41%) |
| Every 100th trade | 34.6 (28.2) | 30.9 (25.1) | 11% (11%) |

The changes of the true price have a variance of $0.5^2 = 0.25$ cents² per trade, and the bounce adds about $s^2/2 = 2$ cents². Sampled every trade, the bounce makes up 89% of the variance of the price changes; sampled every 100th trade, only 11%. In the terms of lecture 17, the bounce is microstructure noise with variance $\omega^2 = s^2/4$, and every price change carries $2\omega^2$ of it. Realized variance, the sum of $n$ squared intraday returns, therefore has a bias of $2n\omega^2$, which grows with the number of returns: sampled too often, it mostly measures noise. Sampling less often removes most of the bias, but leaves fewer returns, so the measure becomes less precise; lecture 17 discusses this trade-off.

## Realized measures from VOLARE

**Exercises:**

7. Read the VOLARE realized measures of the E-mini S&P 500 futures (ES) from `data/volare_realized_measures_daily.parquet`, the rows with `asset_class` `"future"` and `symbol` `"ES"`. In which units are the variances? Compute every day's annualized volatility from `rv5`, plot it over time on a log scale, and compute the volatility of the median day and the median of each year. Which year was the calmest, and which day the most volatile?
8. Noise and jumps: for the 30 Dow Jones stocks in the same file (`asset_class` `"stock"` and `dow30` true), compute the means of `rv1`, `rk`, `bv5`, `rsp5` and `rsn5` relative to the mean of `rv5`, and do the same for ES. What do the ratios tell you about microstructure noise and jumps? Then compute the ratio of the means of `rv1` and `rv5` for each stock and plot it against the stock's median number of trades per day.
9. Compute the realized variance of SPY from five-minute midquote returns of the snapshots of the first part, as in lecture 17, and compare it with `rv5` of ES on the same days. How large are the two volatilities in each March, and how closely do they move together from day to day? Why is the volatility of ES higher? Compare `open_price` of ES with the previous day's `close_price`.

**Solutions:**

VOLARE (Cipollini et al., 2026) is not public: download the files from Absalon into your `data` folder. `volare_realized_measures_daily.parquet` holds one row per asset and trading day, and `asset_class` says whether the asset is a stock or a future. Variances are daily, in squared decimal returns, so $\sqrt{252 \cdot \text{rv5}}$ is the annualized volatility and $10^4 \cdot \text{rv5}$ the variance in squared percent.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-volare-es
library(nanoparquet)
library(slider)

days_per_year <- 252

es <- read_parquet("data/volare_realized_measures_daily.parquet") |>
  filter(asset_class == "future", symbol == "ES") |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(volatility = sqrt(days_per_year * rv5))

es |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = volatility)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Annualized volatility (log scale)")

es |>
  summarize(
    first_day = min(date),
    last_day = max(date),
    days = n(),
    median_volatility = median(volatility),
    most_volatile_day = date[which.max(volatility)],
    highest_volatility = max(volatility)
  )

es |>
  mutate(year = year(date)) |>
  summarize(median_volatility = median(volatility), .by = year)
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-volare-es
from datetime import time

import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from mizani.formatters import percent_format
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf

days_per_year = 252

es = (
    pl.read_parquet("data/volare_realized_measures_daily.parquet")
    .filter(pl.col("asset_class") == "future", pl.col("symbol") == "ES")
    .sort("date")
    .with_columns(volatility=(days_per_year * pl.col("rv5")).sqrt())
)

(
    ggplot(es, aes(x="date", y="volatility"))
    + geom_line(size=0.2)
    + scale_y_log10(labels=percent_format())
    + labs(x="", y="Annualized volatility (log scale)")
)

es.select(
    first_day=pl.col("date").min(),
    last_day=pl.col("date").max(),
    days=pl.len(),
    median_volatility=pl.col("volatility").median(),
    most_volatile_day=pl.col("date").get(pl.col("volatility").arg_max()),
    highest_volatility=pl.col("volatility").max(),
)

es.group_by(year=pl.col("date").dt.year()).agg(
    median_volatility=pl.col("volatility").median()
).sort("year")
```
:::

ES has 4,419 trading days, from 30 September 2009 to 30 October 2026. The median day has an annualized volatility of 11.5%. Volatility changes a lot over time, with calm years such as 2017 (median 6.2%) and turbulent ones such as 2022 (20.4%) and 2020 (17.3%). The most volatile day is 16 March 2020, during the COVID-19 crash, with 126.8%, eleven times the median day.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-volare-measures
dow <- read_parquet("data/volare_realized_measures_daily.parquet") |>
  filter(asset_class == "stock", dow30)

measures <- c("rv1", "rk", "bv5", "rsp5", "rsn5")
relative_to_rv5 <- \(data) {
  data |>
    summarize(across(all_of(measures), \(measure) mean(measure) / mean(rv5)))
}
bind_rows(
  "Dow Jones stocks" = relative_to_rv5(dow),
  ES = relative_to_rv5(es),
  .id = "asset"
)

noise_by_stock <- dow |>
  summarize(
    rv1_to_rv5 = mean(rv1) / mean(rv5),
    trades = median(trades),
    .by = symbol
  )

noise_by_stock |>
  ggplot(aes(x = trades, y = rv1_to_rv5, label = symbol)) +
  geom_text(size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = comma) +
  labs(x = "Median trades per day (log scale)", y = "Mean rv1 / mean rv5")

cor(noise_by_stock$rv1_to_rv5, log(noise_by_stock$trades))
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-volare-measures
dow = pl.read_parquet("data/volare_realized_measures_daily.parquet").filter(
    pl.col("asset_class") == "stock", pl.col("dow30")
)

measures = ["rv1", "rk", "bv5", "rsp5", "rsn5"]


def relative_to_rv5(data):
    return data.select(pl.col(measures).mean() / pl.col("rv5").mean())


pl.concat(
    [
        relative_to_rv5(dow).with_columns(asset=pl.lit("Dow Jones stocks")),
        relative_to_rv5(es).with_columns(asset=pl.lit("ES")),
    ]
)

noise_by_stock = dow.group_by("symbol").agg(
    rv1_to_rv5=pl.col("rv1").mean() / pl.col("rv5").mean(),
    trades=pl.col("trades").median(),
)

(
    ggplot(noise_by_stock, aes(x="trades", y="rv1_to_rv5", label="symbol"))
    + geom_text(size=8)
    + scale_x_log10()
    + labs(x="Median trades per day (log scale)", y="Mean rv1 / mean rv5")
)

noise_by_stock.select(pl.corr("rv1_to_rv5", pl.col("trades").log())).item()
```
:::

The stocks cover 2,975 trading days from 2 January 2015. Relative to `rv5`, the means of the 30 Dow Jones stocks are:

| | `rv1` | `rk` | `bv5` | `rsp5` | `rsn5` |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Dow Jones stocks | 1.09 | 0.97 | 0.89 | 0.50 | 0.50 |
| ES | 1.02 | 0.99 | 0.93 | 0.50 | 0.50 |

- **Noise:** with one-minute returns, the variance is 9% higher than with five-minute returns. This is the bias $2n\omega^2$ of lecture 17, which grows with the number of returns $n$. The realized kernel `rk` removes the noise from one-minute returns and lies close to `rv5`. ES trades far more often than any stock, and its `rv1` is only 2% above `rv5`.
- **Jumps:** bipower variation `bv5` is robust to jumps, `rv5` is not. Their difference suggests that jumps make up about 11% of the variance of the stocks and 7% of ES.
- **Semivariances:** `rsp5` and `rsn5` add up to `rv5`. On average, positive and negative returns contribute the same.

The stocks with few trades have the most noise: the ratio of `rv1` to `rv5` has a correlation of −0.57 with the log number of trades. It is lowest for Amazon (1.02), Microsoft (1.02) and Apple (1.03), and highest for Sherwin-Williams (1.33), the stock with the fewest trades (a median of 16,401 per day).

For SPY, the code of lecture 17 keeps the snapshots of continuous trading, takes the last midquote of every five-minute interval and sums the squared log returns between them within each day.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-spy-es
first_snapshot <- hms::parse_hms("09:30:10")
last_snapshot <- hms::parse_hms("15:59:55")
sampling_interval <- "5 minutes"

spy_rv <- spy |>
  filter(between(hms::as_hms(ts), first_snapshot, last_snapshot)) |>
  mutate(day = as_date(ts), interval = floor_date(ts, sampling_interval)) |>
  summarize(log_price = log(last(midquote)), .by = c(year, day, interval)) |>
  mutate(ret = log_price - lag(log_price), .by = day) |>
  summarize(
    rv = sum(ret^2, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_returns = sum(!is.na(ret)),
    .by = c(year, day)
  )

spy_rv |> filter(rv == 0)

spy_es <- spy_rv |>
  filter(rv > 0) |>
  inner_join(es |> select(day = date, rv5), join_by(day))

spy_es |>
  summarize(
    SPY = sqrt(days_per_year * mean(rv)),
    ES = sqrt(days_per_year * mean(rv5)),
    .by = year
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-year) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = value, color = name)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_log10(labels = percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Annualized volatility (log scale)", color = NULL)

spy_es |>
  summarize(
    days = n(),
    marches = n_distinct(year),
    es_to_spy = mean(rv5) / mean(rv),
    correlation = cor(log(rv), log(rv5))
  )

es |>
  mutate(
    weekday = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1),
    overnight_change = 100 * abs(log(open_price / lag(close_price)))
  ) |>
  summarize(
    median_overnight_change = median(overnight_change, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = weekday
  ) |>
  arrange(weekday)
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-spy-es
first_snapshot = time(9, 30, 10)
last_snapshot = time(15, 59, 55)
sampling_interval = "5m"

spy_rv = (
    spy.filter(pl.col("ts").dt.time().is_between(first_snapshot, last_snapshot))
    .with_columns(
        day=pl.col("ts").dt.date(),
        interval=pl.col("ts").dt.truncate(sampling_interval),
    )
    .group_by("year", "day", "interval", maintain_order=True)
    .agg(log_price=pl.col("midquote").last().log())
    .with_columns(ret=pl.col("log_price").diff().over("day"))
    .group_by("year", "day", maintain_order=True)
    .agg(rv=(pl.col("ret") ** 2).sum(), n_returns=pl.col("ret").count())
)

spy_rv.filter(pl.col("rv") == 0)

spy_es = spy_rv.filter(pl.col("rv") > 0).join(
    es.select(pl.col("date").alias("day"), "rv5"), on="day"
)

spy_es_by_year = spy_es.group_by("year").agg(
    SPY=(days_per_year * pl.col("rv").mean()).sqrt(),
    ES=(days_per_year * pl.col("rv5").mean()).sqrt(),
)
(
    ggplot(
        spy_es_by_year.unpivot(index="year"),
        aes(x="year", y="value", color="variable"),
    )
    + geom_line()
    + geom_point()
    + scale_y_log10(labels=percent_format())
    + labs(x="", y="Annualized volatility (log scale)", color="")
)

spy_es.select(
    days=pl.len(),
    marches=pl.col("year").n_unique(),
    es_to_spy=pl.col("rv5").mean() / pl.col("rv").mean(),
    correlation=pl.corr(pl.col("rv").log(), pl.col("rv5").log()),
)

(
    es.with_columns(
        weekday=pl.col("date").dt.weekday(),
        overnight_change=100
        * (pl.col("open_price") / pl.col("close_price").shift(1)).log().abs(),
    )
    .group_by("weekday")
    .agg(median_overnight_change=pl.col("overnight_change").median())
    .sort("weekday")
)
```
:::

SPY has 388 days with 77 five-minute returns each. One day, 31 March 2022, has a realized variance of zero: in the snapshots of that day, the midquote stops moving a few minutes after the open, a gap in the data. The code leaves this day out. ES starts in September 2009, so the two overlap on 345 days in the 16 Marches from 2010 to 2025.

The two volatilities move together closely: the daily log RVs have a correlation of 0.98, and both are highest in March 2020, with 59.7% for SPY and 83.5% for ES. On the log scale, the two lines run almost parallel: ES is more volatile in every March by a similar factor, for example 9.7% against 7.9% in March 2024. On average, `rv5` of ES is 1.85 times the RV of SPY, between 1.40 (2025) and 2.21 (2011). Both follow the S&P 500, so the difference lies in the hours. From Tuesday to Friday, ES opens at the previous day's close (the median change is zero); only on Mondays, after the weekend, it opens with a gap (median 0.23%). So a day of ES in VOLARE covers the trading of the futures from the evening before, almost 24 hours. The RV of SPY covers only the 6.5 hours of continuous trading, from 9:35 to 16:00. The hours outside, mostly the night, carry about 46% of the variance of ES ($1 - 1/1.85$).

## Forecasting volatility

**Exercises:**

10. Long memory: compute the autocorrelations of $\log \text{rv5}$ of ES up to 252 lags, one year of trading days, and plot them against the lag. Add the autocorrelations of an AR(1) with the same first autocorrelation. What do you see after a week (5 days) and after a month (22 days)?
11. The HAR model (Corsi, 2009): with $RV_t = 10^4 \cdot \text{rv5}$ in squared percent, compute $RV^w_t$ and $RV^m_t$, the averages of the last 5 and 22 days' RV, today included, and the next day's $RV_{t+1}$. Estimate $RV_{t+1} = b_0 + b_d\, RV_t + b_w\, RV^w_t + b_m\, RV^m_t + e_{t+1}$ and the log-HAR, the same regression in $\log RV$, on ES until 31 December 2020. Report the slopes $b_d$, $b_w$ and $b_m$ of both models. Then forecast the next day's RV on every day with these coefficients. Why does the log-HAR forecast need the term $\hat\sigma_e^2/2$?
12. Evaluate the forecasts out of sample, on every day from 2021 on: compute the MSE, $(RV_{t+1} - h_t)^2$, and QLIKE, $RV_{t+1}/h_t - \log(RV_{t+1}/h_t) - 1$, of HAR and log-HAR, and of two simple forecasts: today's RV (a random walk) and the average of the last 22 days. Which forecast wins for ES? Then repeat the steps of tasks 11 and 12 for each of the 30 Dow Jones stocks. For how many stocks does each forecast beat HAR?

**Solutions:**

For an AR(1), the autocorrelation at lag $k$ is the first autocorrelation to the power $k$.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-long-memory
max_lag <- days_per_year

memory <- tibble(
  lag = seq_len(max_lag),
  autocorrelation = acf(log(es$rv5), lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1],
  ar1 = autocorrelation[1]^lag
)

memory |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lag)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = autocorrelation)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ar1), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Lag (trading days)", y = "Autocorrelation of log RV")

memory |> filter(lag %in% c(1, 5, 22, 66, 125, 252))
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-long-memory
max_lag = days_per_year

autocorrelation = acf(es["rv5"].log().to_numpy(), nlags=max_lag)[1:]
memory = pl.DataFrame(
    {"lag": np.arange(1, max_lag + 1), "autocorrelation": autocorrelation}
).with_columns(ar1=autocorrelation[0] ** pl.col("lag"))

(
    ggplot(memory, aes(x="lag"))
    + geom_hline(yintercept=0, size=0.3)
    + geom_line(aes(y="autocorrelation"))
    + geom_line(aes(y="ar1"), linetype="dashed")
    + labs(x="Lag (trading days)", y="Autocorrelation of log RV")
)

memory.filter(pl.col("lag").is_in([1, 5, 22, 66, 125, 252]))
```
:::

The autocorrelation of log RV is 0.81 at lag 1, 0.63 after a week, 0.39 after a month, 0.19 after a quarter (66 days) and 0.11 after half a year (125 days); it reaches zero only after about a year. An AR(1) with the same first autocorrelation is at 0.35 after a week and at 0.01 after a month. Shocks to volatility die out far more slowly than geometrically: volatility has long memory, the pattern the HAR model approximates.

The code follows lecture 17: the rolling means of 5 and 22 days need complete windows, so the first 21 days have no $RV^m_t$, and the last day has no $RV_{t+1}$.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-har
days_week <- 5
days_month <- 22
estimation_end <- ymd("2020-12-31")

har_data <- es |>
  transmute(
    date,
    rv = 1e4 * rv5,
    rv_week = slide_dbl(rv, mean, .before = days_week - 1, .complete = TRUE),
    rv_month = slide_dbl(rv, mean, .before = days_month - 1, .complete = TRUE),
    rv_next = lead(rv)
  ) |>
  drop_na()

estimation <- har_data |> filter(date <= estimation_end)
har <- lm(rv_next ~ rv + rv_week + rv_month, data = estimation)
log_har <- lm(
  log(rv_next) ~ log(rv) + log(rv_week) + log(rv_month),
  data = estimation
)
coef(har)
coef(log_har)
sigma(log_har)^2

har_forecasts <- har_data |>
  mutate(
    har = predict(har, newdata = har_data),
    log_har = exp(predict(log_har, newdata = har_data) + sigma(log_har)^2 / 2)
  )
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-har
days_week = 5
days_month = 22
estimation_end = date(2020, 12, 31)

har_data = (
    es.select("date", rv=1e4 * pl.col("rv5"))
    .with_columns(
        rv_week=pl.col("rv").rolling_mean(days_week),
        rv_month=pl.col("rv").rolling_mean(days_month),
        rv_next=pl.col("rv").shift(-1),
    )
    .drop_nulls()
)

estimation = har_data.filter(pl.col("date") <= estimation_end).to_pandas()
har = smf.ols("rv_next ~ rv + rv_week + rv_month", data=estimation).fit()
log_har = smf.ols(
    "np.log(rv_next) ~ np.log(rv) + np.log(rv_week) + np.log(rv_month)",
    data=estimation,
).fit()
print(har.params, log_har.params, log_har.scale)

har_forecasts = har_data.with_columns(
    har=pl.Series(har.predict(har_data.to_pandas())),
    log_har=pl.Series(
        np.exp(log_har.predict(har_data.to_pandas()) + log_har.scale / 2)
    ),
)
```
:::

The estimation sample has 2,888 days. The slopes $b_d, b_w, b_m$ are 0.53, 0.40 and −0.06 for HAR ($b_0 = 0.15$, $R^2$ of 70%) and 0.55, 0.28 and 0.10 for the log-HAR, as in lecture 17. Both put most weight on today's RV, but the weekly and monthly averages matter as well: the forecast reacts to today's RV and returns slowly to the average of the past weeks. The HAR slope $b_m$ is negative because the COVID-19 crash in March 2020 dominates the regression in levels; lecture 17 shows that the HAR slopes change a lot if the sample ends in 2019, the log-HAR slopes hardly.

The log-HAR forecasts $\log RV_{t+1}$. With normal residuals of variance $\sigma_e^2$, $RV_{t+1}$ is lognormal, and its mean is $\exp(E[\log RV_{t+1}] + \sigma_e^2/2)$. Without the term, $\exp(\widehat{\log RV}_{t+1})$ forecasts the median, which is lower than the mean. The residual variance is 0.30, so the term raises every forecast by 16%.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-forecast-losses
forecast_models <- c("today", "last_22_days", "har", "log_har")

forecast_losses <- function(forecasts) {
  forecasts |>
    filter(date > estimation_end) |>
    mutate(today = rv, last_22_days = rv_month) |>
    pivot_longer(
      all_of(forecast_models),
      names_to = "model",
      values_to = "forecast"
    ) |>
    summarize(
      mse = mean((rv_next - forecast)^2),
      qlike = mean(rv_next / forecast - log(rv_next / forecast) - 1),
      .by = model
    )
}

forecast_losses(har_forecasts)
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-forecast-losses
forecast_models = ["today", "last_22_days", "har", "log_har"]


def forecast_losses(forecasts):
    rv_next = pl.col("rv_next")
    forecast = pl.col("forecast")
    return (
        forecasts.filter(pl.col("date") > estimation_end)
        .with_columns(today=pl.col("rv"), last_22_days=pl.col("rv_month"))
        .unpivot(
            forecast_models,
            index="rv_next",
            variable_name="model",
            value_name="forecast",
        )
        .group_by("model", maintain_order=True)
        .agg(
            mse=((rv_next - forecast) ** 2).mean(),
            qlike=(rv_next / forecast - (rv_next / forecast).log() - 1).mean(),
        )
    )


forecast_losses(har_forecasts)
```
:::

The test sample has 1,509 days, from 4 January 2021 to 29 October 2026. For ES:

| Forecast | MSE | QLIKE |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Today's RV | 3.56 | 0.318 |
| Last 22 days | 3.57 | 0.329 |
| HAR | 2.78 | 0.215 |
| log-HAR | 2.53 | 0.213 |

Both HAR models beat the two simple forecasts by far on both losses, and the log-HAR is a little better than HAR. Today's RV alone is too noisy as a forecast, and the average of the last 22 days reacts too slowly; HAR combines both. The QLIKE of HAR is the 0.215 of lecture 17.

For the Dow Jones stocks, the function `har_forecasts_for()` repeats the steps of task 11 for one stock. The losses of each forecast are then divided by those of HAR for the same stock, so a ratio below 1 means the forecast beats HAR.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```{r}
#| label: r-dow-forecasts
har_forecasts_for <- function(data) {
  har_data <- data |>
    arrange(date) |>
    transmute(
      date,
      rv = 1e4 * rv5,
      rv_week = slide_dbl(rv, mean, .before = days_week - 1, .complete = TRUE),
      rv_month = slide_dbl(
        rv,
        mean,
        .before = days_month - 1,
        .complete = TRUE
      ),
      rv_next = lead(rv)
    ) |>
    drop_na()
  estimation <- har_data |> filter(date <= estimation_end)
  har <- lm(rv_next ~ rv + rv_week + rv_month, data = estimation)
  log_har <- lm(
    log(rv_next) ~ log(rv) + log(rv_week) + log(rv_month),
    data = estimation
  )
  har_data |>
    mutate(
      har = predict(har, newdata = har_data),
      log_har = exp(predict(log_har, newdata = har_data) + sigma(log_har)^2 / 2)
    )
}

dow_losses <- dow |>
  nest(data = -symbol) |>
  mutate(
    losses = map(data, \(data) forecast_losses(har_forecasts_for(data)))
  ) |>
  select(symbol, losses) |>
  unnest(losses)

dow_losses |>
  mutate(
    across(c(mse, qlike), \(loss) loss / loss[model == "har"]),
    .by = symbol
  ) |>
  summarize(
    stocks_better_mse = sum(mse < 1),
    stocks_better_qlike = sum(qlike < 1),
    median_mse = median(mse),
    median_qlike = median(qlike),
    .by = model
  )
```

## Python
```{python}
#| label: py-dow-forecasts
def har_forecasts_for(data):
    har_data = (
        data.sort("date")
        .select("date", rv=1e4 * pl.col("rv5"))
        .with_columns(
            rv_week=pl.col("rv").rolling_mean(days_week),
            rv_month=pl.col("rv").rolling_mean(days_month),
            rv_next=pl.col("rv").shift(-1),
        )
        .drop_nulls()
    )
    estimation = har_data.filter(pl.col("date") <= estimation_end).to_pandas()
    har = smf.ols("rv_next ~ rv + rv_week + rv_month", data=estimation).fit()
    log_har = smf.ols(
        "np.log(rv_next) ~ np.log(rv) + np.log(rv_week) + np.log(rv_month)",
        data=estimation,
    ).fit()
    return har_data.with_columns(
        har=pl.Series(har.predict(har_data.to_pandas())),
        log_har=pl.Series(
            np.exp(log_har.predict(har_data.to_pandas()) + log_har.scale / 2)
        ),
    )


dow_losses = pl.concat(
    forecast_losses(har_forecasts_for(data)).with_columns(symbol=pl.lit(symbol))
    for (symbol,), data in dow.group_by("symbol")
)

losses = pl.col("mse", "qlike")
(
    dow_losses.with_columns(
        losses / losses.filter(pl.col("model") == "har").first().over("symbol")
    )
    .group_by("model", maintain_order=True)
    .agg(
        stocks_better_mse=(pl.col("mse") < 1).sum(),
        stocks_better_qlike=(pl.col("qlike") < 1).sum(),
        median_mse=pl.col("mse").median(),
        median_qlike=pl.col("qlike").median(),
    )
)
```
:::

| Forecast | Stocks better than HAR, MSE | Stocks better than HAR, QLIKE | Median MSE relative to HAR | Median QLIKE relative to HAR |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Today's RV | 0 | 1 | 1.37 | 1.28 |
| Last 22 days | 7 | 0 | 1.07 | 1.23 |
| log-HAR | 29 | 27 | 0.92 | 0.96 |

The results for the stocks are the same as for ES. Today's RV beats HAR only once, on QLIKE for Amazon. The average of the last 22 days beats HAR on MSE for 7 stocks, but never on QLIKE. The log-HAR beats HAR for almost every stock, on QLIKE for 27 of the 30 stocks, as in lecture 17. MSE depends mostly on the few days with extreme RV, QLIKE on the ratio of RV to the forecast, so QLIKE gives every day a similar weight. Lecture 17 also compares the forecasts with GARCH(1,1), which uses only daily returns: HAR beats it on QLIKE for all 30 stocks and for ES.
